title: No 2-state 2-color Turing machine can be universal

fields.label: Label
fields.value: No 2-state 2-color Turing machine can be universal

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: All 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors have behavior too simple to support universality.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: If one looks at the 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors it is fairly easy to see that their behavior is in all cases too simple to support universality.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “Universality in Turing Machines and Other Systems” (from p. 706), p. 708. Scope: 2-state 2-color Turing machines

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-28: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.92

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The machine space is finite and small, and a case-reduced mathematical analysis can settle arbitrary-input capability. Merely observing simple blank-tape traces would be insufficient, but stronger existing methods make the claim resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate all 4096 transition tables modulo relevant symmetries, derive each machine's possible tape dynamics for arbitrary finite input, and prove every case enters a restricted nonuniversal behavior class.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The Turing-machine convention must be fixed.

Blank-tape simulation alone would not rule out universality on encoded inputs.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The space is finite and small, and every machine can be run or decided by existing Busy Beaver methods. Behavior simple enough to decide in closed form cannot implement an arbitrary Turing computation. A full classification either produces a universal machine or a case-by-case proof that none exists, and that work fits in days to weeks.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate all 4096 machines with 2 states and 2 colors and classify each evolution as halting, periodic, or otherwise finitely describable. Confirm if none can emulate a universal system; refute if one machine does.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Wolfram's convention on halting and on head direction must be matched to the enumeration, or the count of 4096 will be partitioned differently.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.95
operationalizability: 0.85
analysis feasibility: 0.9
discriminating power: 0.85
data existence: 0.9

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Every one of the 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colours (Wolfram's convention: each (state, colour) maps to (new colour, new state, move left/right); no halt state) has behaviour that from every finite initial condition becomes eventually periodic, possibly with a drifting head (a 'glider'), after a short transient. Since a universal machine must have initial conditions whose evolution is not eventually periodic (otherwise every question about its evolution is decidable), such a classification is strong evidence that none is universal.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py writes the random initial tapes, compiles tm22.c with gcc and runs it over all 4096 machines x 3176 initial conditions (13,008,896 runs, 10000-step limit). Each run is classified exactly as (A) eventually periodic modulo translation (the head-relative configuration recurs) or (B) escaping, with two exact escape tests: B1 as pre-registered (head beyond all non-zero cells moving outward with a repeated state) and B2 (two successive new-extreme head positions with identical state and identical non-zero tape, the head farther from the tape than the time between them, so the motion repeats verbatim on blank tape). Runs that are neither are put through three post-hoc heuristic classes added after the first full run showed 16% of runs growing their tape: (C) regular linear growth, where the last 16 events at which the head reaches a new extreme position (sampled with stride 1-3) have constant second time differences, constant state and tape contents S_{n+1} = P + S_n[:o] + B + S_n[o:] + Q with fixed P, B, Q, o; (D) the same with event gaps obeying g_{n+1} = a g_n + b, a >= 2 (binary-counter growth); (E) a counter certificate for runs whose tape never grows: at >= 8 returns of the head to one end of its range, in a fixed state, the tape read as a binary number changes by the same non-zero amount. C/D stop the run early once 16 events fit; as a check the program is also run without early stopping (full 10000 steps) on machines 256-319 and 2048-2111 and the class counts compared. Symmetry-distinct machines are counted under state relabelling, colour swap and reflection.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. For each of the 4096 machines and each initial condition in the set I = {every binary tape string of length 1-7 with the head on each of its cells, in each of the 2 states} (1284 initial conditions per machine) plus 100 random tapes of length 16-32 per machine (seeded), simulate on an infinite blank (0) tape for up to 10000 steps and classify the evolution exactly as (A) eventually periodic modulo translation: the head-relative configuration (state, tape between the outermost non-zero cells, head offset) recurs exactly, which implies periodic evolution forever; or (B) escaping: the head is beyond all non-zero cells, moving outward over blank cells, and the same state occurs twice during that outward run, which implies it moves outward forever. 'Supports' if 100% of the (machine, initial condition) pairs are classified as (A) or (B) within 10000 steps, and the largest period found is at most 1000 steps. The symmetry-reduced count of distinct machines (state relabelling, colour swap, reflection) is also computed and compared with Wolfram's 560 as a consistency check on the enumeration.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The test cannot establish universality, so 'refutes' is not reachable by this computation alone. 'Mixed' if any (machine, initial condition) pair is unclassified after 10000 steps (unbounded non-periodic behaviour within the tested inputs, which would be at least consistent with the complexity universality needs) or if periods above 1000 steps occur. 'Supports' otherwise.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of the 13,008,896 (machine, initial condition) runs classified exactly as eventually periodic (A) or escaping (B) within 10000 steps (pre-registered threshold 1.0)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: exact for A and B; C, D and E are heuristic pattern fits (see caveats)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Too simple to support universality' is operationalized as: every tested evolution is provably eventually periodic (with or without drift), established by exact recurrence detection rather than by visual inspection. This is necessary-condition evidence: universality requires some input with a non-eventually-periodic evolution, and the tested inputs cover all short tapes exhaustively plus random longer ones, but not all inputs; a proof for all inputs would need a per-machine argument. The convention follows NKS p. 78 and the note 'Turing machine enumeration' (p. 1120): machines never halt, and all 4096 = 8^4 rule tables are counted. The search program is in C (compiled by analysis.py with gcc) for speed; this tooling deviation is recorded.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
All 2-state 2-colour Turing machines (generated by analysis.py + tm22.c)

NKS note 'Turing machine enumeration' (p. 1120)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The pre-registered criterion fails: only 83.36% of runs are eventually periodic (A) or escaping (B); analysis.py reports preregistered_verdict = 'mixed'. The pre-registered hypothesis was too narrow, not the claim: the remaining runs are tapes that grow forever in a regular way (a head sweeping a growing block, 2,142,325 runs in 864 machines) or binary counters (22,536 runs in 11 machines belonging to just 2 symmetry classes, representatives 441 and 462), which Wolfram describes as the most complex 2,2 behaviour (NKS p. 79-80, 'nested'). Under the post-hoc classes C-E every run but 2 of 13,008,896 is accounted for, and both residual runs belong to counter machines (1372, 3654) whose other 3175 runs are classified; the verdict 'supports' rests on these post-hoc classes and is therefore given lower confidence.

Classes A and B are proofs of the individual run's future; classes C, D and E are pattern fits over a finite window (16 growth events, or 8 counter visits) and could in principle be fooled by behaviour that changes later. The no-early-stop check on 128 machines gives identical class counts, and the classes were designed after inspecting the actual mechanisms (sweepers, binary counters), but they are heuristics.

The computation is necessary-condition evidence only: it covers all tapes of length <= 7 and 100 random longer tapes per machine, not all inputs, and finding only repetitive and nested behaviour does not prove non-universality. The known proof is Pavlotskaya (1973), who showed every 2-state 2-colour machine has a decidable halting problem; that result is not checked here.

Implementation deviations from the pre-registration: the exhaustive set has 3076 initial conditions per machine, not 1284 (miscount in the pre-registration; the set itself is as described); the A test is applied for t <= 2000 and spans <= 128 only (for speed; no run escaped A because of this: the max transient to A or B is 3354 for B, and the max period is 24); an additional exact escape test B2 was added because many 'glider' runs carry a bounded pattern away from a fixed tape remnant and are neither periodic modulo translation nor caught by B1. The search is in C (gcc), a tooling deviation from the python/mjs rule, recorded in the pre-registration.

The symmetry-reduced count of 560 distinct machines matches Wolfram's note (p. 1120), confirming the enumeration covers the same family.
